# Appendix F: Compile Errors

Every error the compiler is tested for, grouped by feature: a program that triggers it, the part of the message the test checks, what went wrong, and a version that compiles. The full message also names the file and line, and often suggests the fix. The programs come from `tests/errors/` and `tests/errors_pkg/`, so this page lists exactly what the compiler reports.

- [`do!` blocks](#do-blocks): 7 errors
- [Anonymous struct literals](#anonymous-struct-literals): 4 errors
- [Closures](#closures): 28 errors
- [Comptime and macros](#comptime-and-macros): 28 errors
- [Declarations and parsing](#declarations-and-parsing): 3 errors
- [Destructors](#destructors): 46 errors
- [Error handling](#error-handling): 8 errors
- [Interfaces](#interfaces): 42 errors
- [Optimization attributes](#optimization-attributes): 17 errors
- [Packages and imports](#packages-and-imports): 7 errors

## `do!` blocks

### do after call

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
side :: proc() -> int { return 1 }
main :: proc() {
	n := side() + do! { take 1 }
	_ = n
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
do! would run before 'side()', which comes first in the statement
```

The `do!` block runs before the statement it's in, so here it would run before `side()`, out of order. Compute it in a statement of its own:

```vidar
side :: proc() -> int { return 1 }

main :: proc() {
	s := side()
	n := s + do! { take 1 }
	_ = n
}
```

### do in defer

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
import "core:fmt"
main :: proc() {
	defer fmt.println(do! { take 1 })
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
do! can only be used in a declaration, an assignment, an expression statement or a return
```

A deferred statement runs later, but the `do!` block would run now. Compute the value first:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	v := do! { take 1 }
	defer fmt.println(v)
}
```

### do no take

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	x := do! { y := 1; _ = y }
	_ = x
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
do!: the block needs a 'take value'
```

A `do!` block is a value, and gives it with `take`:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	x := do! { y := 1; take y }
	_ = x
}
```

### do short circuit

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	ready := false
	ok := ready && do! { take true }
	_ = ok
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
do! would run before the statement, even when the right side of '&&' is skipped
```

The `do!` block would run even when `&&` skips its right side. Compute it in a statement of its own, under an `if` if it must not always run:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	ready := false
	ok := false
	if ready do ok = do! { take true }
	_ = ok
}
```

### do take in nested proc

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	n := do! {
		f := proc() -> int { take 1 }
		take f()
	}
	_ = n
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'take' gives the value of a do! { ... } or comptime! { ... } block, and cannot be used in a proc nested inside it
```

`take` gives the value of the `do!` block it's directly in; a procedure inside the block returns with `return`:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	n := do! {
		f := proc() -> int { return 1 }
		take f()
	}
	_ = n
}
```

### do ternary branch

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	n := 1 if true else do! { take 2 }
	_ = n
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
do! would run before the statement, even when its branch of the ternary is not taken
```

The `do!` block would run even when its branch isn't taken. Use an `if` statement:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	n := 1
	if !true do n = do! { take 2 }
	_ = n
}
```

### do two values

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	x := do! { take 1, 2 }
	_ = x
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
do!: 'take' takes exactly one value
```

A `do!` block has one value. To give several, take a struct:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	x := do! {
		pair := [2]int{1, 2}
		take pair
	}
	_ = x
}
```

## Anonymous struct literals

### anon struct duplicate field

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	a := { x = 1, x = 2 }
	_ = a
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
field 'x' is given twice
```

An anonymous struct literal declares one field per name, so a name given twice would be two fields with the same name. Give each field once, or use two names:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	a := { x = 1, y = 2 }
	_ = a
}
```

### anon struct nested positional

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	a := { pos = { 1, 2 } }
	_ = a
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
the type of field 'pos' cannot be inferred; write the literal's type
```

A field's type comes from its value, and a positional literal like `{ 1, 2 }` doesn't say what type it is. Name the nested literal's fields, so it becomes an anonymous struct too, or write its type:

```vidar
Point :: struct { x, y: int }

main :: proc() {
	a := { pos = { x = 1, y = 2 } }
	b := { pos = Point{1, 2} }
	_, _ = a, b
}
```

### anon struct nil

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	a := { p = nil }
	_ = a
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
the type of field 'p' cannot be inferred from 'nil'
```

`nil` is the zero value of many types, so it can't say which one the field should have. Give the value a type:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	a := { p = (^int)(nil) }
	_ = a
}
```

### anon struct unnamed field

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	a := { x = 1, 2 }
	_ = a
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
every element of an anonymous struct literal needs a field name
```

An anonymous struct's fields are named by its literal, so every element needs `name = value`:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	a := { x = 1, y = 2 }
	_ = a
}
```

## Closures

### capture global

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
G := 1
main :: proc() { f := proc[G]() {} }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
is not a local variable; closures can use globals and constants without capturing them
```

Only locals are captured. A global (or a constant) is visible from the closure's body without capturing it, so take it out of the capture list:

```vidar
G := 1

main :: proc() {
	f := proc[]() -> int { return G }
	_ = f
}
```

### closure capture const local

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	K :: 3
	f := proc[K]() {}
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
is not a local variable; closures can use globals and constants without capturing them
```

A local constant isn't a variable: the closure's body can use it without capturing it.

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	K :: 3
	f := proc[]() -> int { return K }
	_ = f
}
```

### closure capture field write

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Point :: struct { x, y: int }
main :: proc() {
	p := Point{1, 2}
	move := proc[p]() { p.x += 1 }
	_ = move
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'p' is captured by value: each call gets a fresh copy
```

A by-value capture is a copy that each call gets afresh, so writing to it (or to one of its fields) would be lost. Capture a pointer to change the original:

```vidar
Point :: struct { x, y: int }

main :: proc() {
	p := Point{1, 2}
	move := proc[&p]() { p.x += 1 }
	move()
	_ = p
}
```

### closure capture twice

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	n := 1
	f := proc[n, &n]() {}
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'n' is captured twice
```

Each name appears once in a capture list. Capture it by value or by pointer, not both:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	n := 1
	f := proc[&n]() { n += 1 }
	_ = f
}
```

### closure capture unknown

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	f := proc[zz]() {}
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
cannot capture unknown name 'zz'
```

The capture list names a variable that doesn't exist. Check the spelling, or declare it first:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	zz := 1
	f := proc[zz]() -> int { return zz }
	_ = f
}
```

### closure capture write

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	n := 1
	counter := proc[n]() -> int { n += 1; return n }
	_ = counter
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'n' is captured by value: each call gets a fresh copy
```

A by-value capture is read-only: each call gets a fresh copy, so a change would be lost. Capture `&n` to change the variable itself:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	n := 1
	counter := proc[&n]() -> int { n += 1; return n }
	_ = counter
}
```

### closure captures closure

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
twice :: proc(f: closure(int) -> int) -> closure(int) -> int {
	return proc[f](x: int) -> int { return f(f(x)) }
}
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'f' is a closure, and a closure can't hold a copy of another one
```

A closure has a fixed amount of room for captures, so it can't hold a copy of another closure. Capture a pointer to it: a heap copy from `new_clone` when the new closure outlives this procedure.

```vidar
twice :: proc(f: closure(int) -> int) -> closure(int) -> int {
	fp := new_clone(f)
	return proc[fp](x: int) -> int { return fp^(fp^(x)) }
}

main :: proc() {}
```

### closure named args

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	f := proc[](a: int) {}
	f(a = 1)
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
named arguments are not supported when calling closures
```

Calls through a closure pass their arguments by position:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	f := proc[](a: int) {}
	f(1)
}
```

### closure needs body

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	x := 1
	f := proc[x]()
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
closure literal needs a body
```

A capture list makes a closure literal, which needs a body in braces. For a closure type, write `closure(...)`:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	x := 1
	f := proc[x]() -> int { return x }
	_ = f
}
```

### closure outer proc local

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	x := 1
	outer := proc[]() {
		inner := proc[x]() {}
	}
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'x' belongs to an outer procedure; capture it there first
```

A closure can capture only the locals of the procedure it's written in, or what its enclosing closure captured. Capture `x` in the outer closure first:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	x := 1
	outer := proc[x]() {
		inner := proc[x]() -> int { return x }
		_ = inner
	}
	_ = outer
}
```

### closure ref append

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

World :: struct { on_frame: [dynamic]closure(frame: int) }

run :: proc(w: ^World) {
	ticks := 0
	append(&w.on_frame, proc[&ticks](frame: int) { ticks += 1 })
}

main :: proc() {
	w: World
	run(&w)
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &ticks and is appended to memory behind a pointer (line 8)
```

The closure holds `&ticks`, a local of `run`, and would be kept in `w.on_frame` after `run` returns. Keep the state on the heap and capture that pointer instead:

```vidar
World :: struct { on_frame: [dynamic]closure(frame: int) }

run :: proc(w: ^World) {
	ticks := new_clone(0)
	append(&w.on_frame, proc[ticks](frame: int) { ticks^ += 1 })
}

main :: proc() {
	w: World
	run(&w)
}
```

### closure ref env copy

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

outer :: proc(k: int) -> closure() -> closure() -> int {
	return proc[k]() -> closure() -> int {
		// k here is this closure's own copy, which is gone once it returns
		return proc[&k]() -> int { return k }
	}
}

main :: proc() { _ = outer(1) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &k and is returned (line 7)
```

Inside the outer closure, `k` is that closure's own copy, which is gone when its call returns, so the inner closure can't hold `&k`. Capture `k` by value:

```vidar
outer :: proc(k: int) -> closure() -> closure() -> int {
	return proc[k]() -> closure() -> int {
		return proc[k]() -> int { return k }
	}
}

main :: proc() { _ = outer(1) }
```

### closure ref field

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

Button :: struct { on_click: closure() }

wire :: proc(b: ^Button) {
	hits := 0
	b.on_click = proc[&hits]() { hits += 1 }
}

main :: proc() {
	b: Button
	wire(&b)
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &hits and is stored in memory behind a pointer (line 8)
```

The closure holds `&hits`, a local of `wire`, and is stored in a struct the caller keeps. Put the count on the heap:

```vidar
Button :: struct { on_click: closure() }

wire :: proc(b: ^Button) {
	hits := new_clone(0)
	b.on_click = proc[hits]() { hits^ += 1 }
}

main :: proc() {
	b: Button
	wire(&b)
}
```

### closure ref global

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

on_tick: closure()

install :: proc() {
	hits := 0
	on_tick = proc[&hits]() { hits += 1 }
}

main :: proc() { install() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &hits and is stored in a global (line 8)
```

A global outlives every procedure, so it can't hold a closure that points at a local. Use a global for the state too, which needs no capture, or a heap pointer:

```vidar
on_tick: closure()
hits: int

install :: proc() {
	on_tick = proc[]() { hits += 1 }
}

main :: proc() { install() }
```

### closure ref named result

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

counter :: proc() -> (f: closure() -> int) {
	n := 0
	f = proc[&n]() -> int { n += 1; return n }
	return
}

main :: proc() { _ = counter() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &n and is returned (line 6)
```

Assigning a closure to a named result returns it, so it can't hold `&n` of a local. Capture a heap pointer:

```vidar
counter :: proc() -> (f: closure() -> int) {
	n := new_clone(0)
	f = proc[n]() -> int { n^ += 1; return n^ }
	return
}

main :: proc() { _ = counter() }
```

### closure ref param

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

every :: proc(n: int, f: closure(t: int)) -> closure(t: int) {
	return proc[n, &f](t: int) { if t % n == 0 do f(t) }
}

main :: proc() { _ = every(2, proc[](t: int) {}) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
Capture a pointer from new_clone(f) instead
```

A parameter lives in the procedure's frame like a local, so a returned closure can't hold `&f`. Make a heap copy and capture that:

```vidar
every :: proc(n: int, f: closure(t: int)) -> closure(t: int) {
	fp := new_clone(f)
	return proc[n, fp](t: int) { if t % n == 0 do fp^(t) }
}

main :: proc() { _ = every(2, proc[](t: int) {}) }
```

### closure ref passed chain

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

Handlers :: struct { all: [dynamic]closure() }

keep :: proc(hs: ^Handlers, f: closure()) {
	append(&hs.all, f)
}

later :: proc(hs: ^Handlers, f: closure()) {
	keep(hs, f)
}

register :: proc(hs: ^Handlers) {
	n := 0
	g := proc[&n]() { n += 1 }
	later(hs, g)
}

main :: proc() {
	hs: Handlers
	register(&hs)
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &n and is passed to later (line 17), where it is passed to keep (line 11), where it is appended to memory behind a pointer (line 7)
```

Vidar follows the closure through `later` and `keep`, and finds that it ends up in `hs.all`, which outlives `register`. Give the closure state that lives as long:

```vidar
Handlers :: struct { all: [dynamic]closure() }

keep :: proc(hs: ^Handlers, f: closure()) {
	append(&hs.all, f)
}

later :: proc(hs: ^Handlers, f: closure()) {
	keep(hs, f)
}

register :: proc(hs: ^Handlers) {
	n := new_clone(0)
	g := proc[n]() { n^ += 1 }
	later(hs, g)
}

main :: proc() {
	hs: Handlers
	register(&hs)
}
```

### closure ref passed go

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "vidar:sched"

start :: proc() {
	n := 0
	sched.go(proc[&n]() { n += 1 })
}

main :: proc() { start() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &n and is passed to sched.go (line 8), which runs it on a goroutine that can outlive this proc
```

A goroutine can run after `start` has returned, so it can't hold `&n` of `start`'s locals. Share heap state instead (or start the goroutine from `main`, whose locals live until the program exits):

```vidar
import "vidar:sched"

start :: proc() {
	n := new_clone(0)
	sched.go(proc[n]() { n^ += 1 })
}

main :: proc() { start() }
```

### closure ref passed named

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "vidar:sched"

spawn :: proc(task: closure(), times := 1) {
	for _ in 0..<times do sched.go(task)
}

start :: proc() {
	n := 0
	f := proc[&n]() { n += 1 }
	spawn(times = 2, task = f)
}

main :: proc() { start() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &n and is passed to spawn (line 13), where it is passed to sched.go (line 7), which runs it on a goroutine
```

`spawn` passes its `task` parameter to `sched.go`, so passing it a closure that holds `&n` lets that pointer reach a goroutine. Use heap state:

```vidar
import "vidar:sched"

spawn :: proc(task: closure(), times := 1) {
	for _ in 0..<times do sched.go(task)
}

start :: proc() {
	n := new_clone(0)
	f := proc[n]() { n^ += 1 }
	spawn(times = 2, task = f)
}

main :: proc() { start() }
```

### closure ref passed returned

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

id :: proc(f: closure() -> int) -> closure() -> int { return f }

counter :: proc() -> closure() -> int {
	n := 0
	f := id(proc[&n]() -> int { n += 1; return n })
	return f
}

main :: proc() { _ = counter() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &n and is returned (line 9)
```

`id` returns its parameter, so `f` is the same closure, holding `&n`, and returning it lets it outlive `n`. Capture a heap pointer:

```vidar
id :: proc(f: closure() -> int) -> closure() -> int { return f }

counter :: proc() -> closure() -> int {
	n := new_clone(0)
	f := id(proc[n]() -> int { n^ += 1; return n^ })
	return f
}

main :: proc() { _ = counter() }
```

### closure ref passed store

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

saved: closure()

keep :: proc(f: closure()) {
	saved = f
}

start :: proc() {
	n := 0
	keep(proc[&n]() { n += 1 })
}

main :: proc() { start() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &n and is passed to keep (line 12), where it is stored in a global (line 7)
```

`keep` stores its parameter in a global, so the closure passed to it can't hold `&n` of a local:

```vidar
saved: closure()

keep :: proc(f: closure()) {
	saved = f
}

start :: proc() {
	n := new_clone(0)
	keep(proc[n]() { n^ += 1 })
}

main :: proc() { start() }
```

### closure ref returned

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

counter :: proc() -> closure() -> int {
	n := 0
	return proc[&n]() -> int { n += 1; return n }
}

main :: proc() { _ = counter() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &n and is returned (line 6)
```

`n` lives in `counter`'s frame, which is gone once it returns, so the returned closure can't point at it. Keep the state on the heap:

```vidar
counter :: proc() -> closure() -> int {
	n := new_clone(0)
	return proc[n]() -> int { n^ += 1; return n^ }
}

main :: proc() { _ = counter() }
```

### closure ref returned local

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

counter :: proc() -> closure() -> int {
	n := 0
	f := proc[&n]() -> int { n += 1; return n }
	g := f
	return g
}

main :: proc() { _ = counter() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &n and is returned (line 8)
```

Copying the closure into another local doesn't change what it points at: `g` still holds `&n`. Keep the state on the heap:

```vidar
counter :: proc() -> closure() -> int {
	n := new_clone(0)
	f := proc[n]() -> int { n^ += 1; return n^ }
	g := f
	return g
}

main :: proc() { _ = counter() }
```

### closure ref struct lit

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

Handler :: struct { on: closure() }

make_handler :: proc() -> Handler {
	hits := 0
	return Handler{on = proc[&hits]() { hits += 1 }}
}

main :: proc() { _ = make_handler() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &hits and is returned (line 8)
```

Returning a struct that holds the closure returns the closure. Keep the state on the heap:

```vidar
Handler :: struct { on: closure() }

make_handler :: proc() -> Handler {
	hits := new_clone(0)
	return Handler{on = proc[hits]() { hits^ += 1 }}
}

main :: proc() { _ = make_handler() }
```

### closure type switch by ref

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	u: union { int, string } = 1
	switch v in u {
	case int:
		f := proc[&v]() {}
	}
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'v' cannot be captured by reference
```

The variable a type switch binds is a copy that Odin doesn't let you take the address of. Capture it by value, or capture the union itself by pointer:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	u: union { int, string } = 1
	#partial switch v in u {
	case int:
		f := proc[v]() -> int { return v }
		g := proc[&u]() { u = 2 }
		_, _ = f, g
	}
}
```

### nested plain proc

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	x := 1
	f := proc() -> int { return x }
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
nested procs cannot see it. Use a closure
```

A procedure literal without a capture list is plain Odin, and can't see the enclosing procedure's locals. Make it a closure that captures what it uses:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	x := 1
	f := proc[x]() -> int { return x }
	_ = f
}
```

### not captured

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	x := 1
	f := proc[]() -> int { return x }
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'x' is a local of the enclosing procedure and is not captured
```

A closure can only use the outer locals it captures. Add `x` to the capture list:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	x := 1
	f := proc[x]() -> int { return x }
	_ = f
}
```

### closure ref passed pkg

This program doesn't compile:

<span class="filename">Filename: events/events.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package events

handler: closure()

on :: proc(f: closure()) {
	handler = f
}

fire :: proc() {
	handler()
}
```

<span class="filename">Filename: main.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "events"

listen :: proc() {
	hits := 0
	events.on(proc[&hits]() { hits += 1 })
}

main :: proc() {
	listen()
	events.fire()
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure captures &hits and is passed to events.on (line 8), where it is stored in a global (events.vidar:6)
```

`events.on` stores its closure in a package-level variable, so the closure outlives `listen`, and can't hold `&hits`. Vidar follows the call into the other package to find that out. Keep the count on the heap:

```vidar,project=err-closure-ref-passed-pkg,file=main.vidar
package main

import "events"

listen :: proc() {
	hits := new_clone(0)
	events.on(proc[hits]() { hits^ += 1 })
}

main :: proc() {
	listen()
	events.fire()
}
```

```vidar,project=err-closure-ref-passed-pkg,file=events/events.vidar
package events

handler: closure()

on :: proc(f: closure()) {
	handler = f
}

fire :: proc() {
	handler()
}
```

## Comptime and macros

### compile error builtin

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
make_scaler :: proc!(T: Type) -> Expr {
	if type_name(T) == "string" { compile_error("make_scaler: cannot scale a string") }
	return quote(1)
}
main :: proc() { _ = make_scaler!(string) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
make_scaler: cannot scale a string
```

The macro rejected its argument on purpose, with `compile_error`. Pass it something it accepts:

```vidar
make_scaler :: proc!(T: Type) -> Expr {
	if type_name(T) == "string" { compile_error("make_scaler: cannot scale a string") }
	return quote(1)
}

main :: proc() { _ = make_scaler!(f64) }
```

### comptime anon proc

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	f := proc!(n: int) -> int { return n }
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
comptime procs are declared as name :: proc!(...) { ... }
```

A comptime procedure is a declaration, `name :: proc!(...)`, at file scope or in a procedure; it can't be a value assigned to a variable:

```vidar
double :: proc!(n: int) -> int { return n * 2 }

main :: proc() {
	f := double!(4)
	_ = f
}
```

### comptime bang not proc

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
fib! :: proc(n: int) -> int { return n }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
comptime procs are declared as name :: proc!(...) { ... }
```

The `!` goes after `proc` in the declaration, and after the name only at the call:

```vidar
fib :: proc!(n: int) -> int { return n }

main :: proc() { _ = fib!(3) }
```

### comptime block no value

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	x := comptime! { y := 1; _ = y }
	_ = x
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
comptime!: the block needs a single expression or a 'take value'
```

A `comptime!` block is a value, so it needs one: a single expression, or `take value` at the end:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	x := comptime! { y := 1; take y + 1 }
	_ = x
}
```

### comptime block runtime value

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	n := 4
	x := comptime! {
		total := 0
		for i in 1..=n do total += i
		take total
	}
	_ = x
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
comptime!: cannot be evaluated at compile time: 'n' is a runtime value
```

`n` only has a value when the program runs. Make it a constant, or compute the value at run time:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	N :: 4
	x := comptime! {
		total := 0
		for i in 1..=N do total += i
		take total
	}
	_ = x
}
```

### comptime call compile error

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
check :: proc!(n: int) -> int {
	if n > 3 do compile_error("too big")
	return n
}
main :: proc() {
	x := check!(5)
	_ = x
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
in expansion of 'check!': too big
```

The macro rejected its argument on purpose, with `compile_error`. Pass it something it accepts:

```vidar
check_small :: proc!(n: int) -> int {
	if n > 3 do compile_error("too big")
	return n
}

main :: proc() {
	x := check_small!(2)
	_ = x
}
```

### comptime call no value

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
noop :: proc() {}
main :: proc() {
	x := noop!()
	_ = x
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'noop!' has no value
```

`name!(...)` used as a value puts the procedure's result in its place, and `noop` has none. Call it as a statement, or give it a result:

```vidar
seven :: proc() -> int { return 7 }

main :: proc() {
	x := seven!()
	_ = x
}
```

### comptime call runtime value

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
square :: proc(x: int) -> int { return x * x }
main :: proc() {
	k := 3
	x := square!(k)
	_ = x
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'square!' cannot run at compile time: 'k' is a runtime value
```

`square!(k)` runs `square` while compiling, when `k` has no value yet. Call it at run time, without the `!`, or pass a constant:

```vidar
square :: proc(x: int) -> int { return x * x }

main :: proc() {
	k := 3
	x := square(k)
	y := square!(3)
	_, _ = x, y
}
```

### comptime old syntax

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
fib :: comptime proc(n: int) -> int { return n }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
comptime procs are declared as name :: proc!(...) { ... }
```

Comptime procedures are declared with a `!` after `proc`:

```vidar
fib :: proc!(n: int) -> int { return n }

main :: proc() { _ = fib!(3) }
```

### comptime proc runtime call

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
fib :: proc!(n: int) -> int { return n }
main :: proc() {
	k := 3
	x := fib(k)
	_ = x
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'fib' is a comptime proc
```

A procedure declared with `proc!` only exists while compiling, so it's called with a `!` and constant arguments. For a run-time call, declare it with `proc`:

```vidar
fib :: proc(n: int) -> int { return n }

main :: proc() {
	k := 3
	x := fib(k)
	y := fib!(3)
	_, _ = x, y
}
```

### comptime return in block

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	x := comptime! { y := 2; return y * 2 }
	_ = x
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
comptime!: use 'take value' to give the block its value
```

`return` would leave the enclosing procedure; a `comptime!` block gives its value with `take`:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	x := comptime! { y := 2; take y * 2 }
	_ = x
}
```

### comptime unknown

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	x := squre!(3)
	_ = x
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'squre' is not declared
```

Nothing called `squre` is declared: probably a typo.

```vidar
square :: proc(x: int) -> int { return x * x }

main :: proc() {
	x := square!(3)
	_ = x
}
```

### macro arg type

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
square :: proc!(x: Expr(i32)) -> Expr(i32) { return quote($x * $x) }
main :: proc() { _ = square!("hi") }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
argument 'x' has type untyped string but the macro expects i32
```

The macro's parameter is `Expr(i32)`, so its argument must be an expression of type `i32`:

```vidar
square :: proc!(x: Expr(i32)) -> Expr(i32) { return quote($x * $x) }

main :: proc() { _ = square!(3) }
```

### macro arg typed var

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
square :: proc!(x: Expr(i32)) -> Expr(i32) { return quote($x * $x) }
main :: proc() { v: f64 = 2; _ = square!(v) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
argument 'x' has type f64 but the macro expects i32
```

`v` is an `f64`, and the macro takes an `i32`. Convert the argument, or declare the variable with the right type:

```vidar
square :: proc!(x: Expr(i32)) -> Expr(i32) { return quote($x * $x) }

main :: proc() {
	v: f64 = 2
	_ = square!(i32(v))
}
```

### macro bad splice

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
bad :: proc!() -> Expr { return quote($ + 1) }
main :: proc() { _ = bad!() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
expected an identifier or '(' after '$'
```

Inside a quote, `$` is followed by a name, `$x`, or a parenthesized compile-time expression, `$(x + 1)`. For a literal `$`, write `$$`:

```vidar
one :: proc!() -> Expr { n := 1; return quote($n + 1) }

main :: proc() { _ = one!() }
```

### macro division by zero

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
d :: proc!(n: int) -> int { return 10 / n }
main :: proc() { _ = d!(0) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
division by zero at compile time
```

The macro divided by zero while compiling. Check the argument first, and report a clearer error:

```vidar
d :: proc!(n: int) -> int {
	if n == 0 do compile_error("d!: n must not be 0")
	return 10 / n
}

main :: proc() { _ = d!(2) }
```

### macro fields of non struct

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
f :: proc!(T: Type) -> int { return len(type_fields(T)) }
main :: proc() { _ = f!([4]int) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'[4]int' is not a struct type
```

`type_fields` lists a struct's fields, and an array has none. Pass a struct type:

```vidar
f :: proc!(T: Type) -> int { return len(type_fields(T)) }

Point :: struct { x, y: int }

main :: proc() { _ = f!(Point) }
```

### macro ident list not names

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

fn :: proc!(captures: []Ident, body: Stmt) -> Expr {
	return quote(proc[$captures]() { $body })
}

main :: proc() {
	a := 1
	f := fn!({a + 1}) {}
	f()
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
argument 'captures' must be a list of identifiers, like {a, &b}
```

A `[]Ident` parameter takes a list of names, each optionally with `&`. Compute the value first, and pass its name:

```vidar
fn :: proc!(captures: []Ident, body: Stmt) -> Expr {
	return quote(proc[$captures]() { $body })
}

main :: proc() {
	a := 1
	b := a + 1
	f := fn!({b}) {}
	f()
}
```

### macro ident param

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
decl :: proc!(name: Ident) -> Stmt { return quote { $name := 1 } }
main :: proc() { decl!(a + b) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
argument 'name' must be an identifier
```

An `Ident` parameter takes a bare name:

```vidar
decl :: proc!(name: Ident) -> Stmt { return quote { $name := 1 } }

main :: proc() {
	decl!(total)
	_ = total
}
```

### macro index out of bounds

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
f :: proc!() -> int { xs := [dynamic]int{1, 2}; return xs[3] }
main :: proc() { _ = f!() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
index 3 out of bounds (len 2)
```

Compile-time code is bounds-checked like run-time code. Index within the array:

```vidar
f :: proc!() -> int { xs := [dynamic]int{1, 2}; return xs[1] }

main :: proc() { _ = f!() }
```

### macro reads runtime global

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
counter := 5
get :: proc!() -> int { return counter }
main :: proc() { _ = get!() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'counter' is a runtime variable and is not available at compile time
```

A global variable only has its value at run time. Make it a constant, or pass the value in:

```vidar
COUNTER :: 5

get :: proc!() -> int { return COUNTER }

main :: proc() { _ = get!() }
```

### macro recursive

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
loop :: proc!(x: Expr) -> Expr { return quote(loop!($x)) }
main :: proc() { _ = loop!(1) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
macro expansion too deep
```

The macro's expansion calls the macro again, forever. Give the recursion a base case that returns plain code:

```vidar
times :: proc!(n: int, x: Expr) -> Expr {
	if n <= 1 do return x
	return quote($x + times!($(n - 1), $x))
}

main :: proc() { _ = times!(3, 2) }
```

### macro returns type

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
t :: proc!() -> Type { return int }
main :: proc() { _ = t!() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
macros cannot return Type
```

A macro's result is code or a value, not a type. Return an expression that uses the type:

```vidar
zero_int :: proc!() -> Expr { return quote(int(0)) }

main :: proc() { _ = zero_int!() }
```

### macro runtime arg

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
twice :: proc!(n: int) -> int { return n * 2 }
main :: proc() { n := 3; _ = twice!(n) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
must be a compile-time constant
```

A plain parameter type takes a compile-time constant, and `n` is a run-time variable. Pass a constant, or take the argument as code with `Expr`:

```vidar
twice :: proc!(n: Expr) -> Expr { return quote($n * 2) }

main :: proc() {
	n := 3
	_ = twice!(n)
}
```

### macro step limit

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
spin :: proc!() -> int { i := 0; for { i += 1 }; return i }
main :: proc() { _ = spin!() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
exceeded the step limit
```

The macro's body ran too long, which usually means a loop that never ends. Give the loop an end:

```vidar
count_to :: proc!(n: int) -> int {
	i := 0
	for i < n do i += 1
	return i
}

main :: proc() { _ = count_to!(10) }
```

### macro void in expr

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
noop :: proc!() { }
main :: proc() { x := noop!() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
returns nothing and can only be used as a statement
```

A macro without a result can only be a statement. Call it as one, or give it a result:

```vidar
noop :: proc!() { }

main :: proc() {
	noop!()
}
```

### macro wrong arity

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
twice :: proc!(x: Expr) -> Expr { return quote($x * 2) }
main :: proc() { _ = twice!(1, 2) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
macro 'twice' expects 1 argument(s) but got 2
```

The macro takes one argument. Pass one, or give the macro a second parameter:

```vidar
twice :: proc!(x: Expr) -> Expr { return quote($x * 2) }

main :: proc() { _ = twice!(1) }
```

### stmt macro in expr

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
noop :: proc!() -> Stmt { return quote { x := 1 } }
main :: proc() { y := noop!() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
returns Stmt and can only be used as a statement
```

A macro returning `Stmt` produces statements, which can't be a value. Call it as a statement, or return an `Expr`:

```vidar
one :: proc!() -> Expr { return quote(1) }

main :: proc() { y := one!(); _ = y }
```

## Declarations and parsing

### duplicate global

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
x :: 1
x :: 2
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'x' is already declared in package 'main'
```

Two declarations at file scope have the same name. Rename one:

```vidar
x :: 1
y :: 2

main :: proc() {}
```

### parse attribute without decl

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	@(private) x = 1
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
attributes must precede a declaration
```

An attribute describes a declaration, and an assignment isn't one. Declare the variable:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	@(static) x := 1
	_ = x
}
```

### parse unterminated block

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	x := 1
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
unterminated block
```

A `{` is missing its `}`:

```vidar
main :: proc() {
	x := 1
	_ = x
}
```

## Destructors

### destroy append copy

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

main :: proc() {
	files: [dynamic]File
	f := open("a")
	append(&files, f)
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
append would copy it
```

Appending `f` would put a copy in the array while `f` keeps its own, and both would be destroyed. Move it in, or append a new value directly:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
main :: proc() {
	files: [dynamic]File
	f := open("a")
	append(&files, move!(f))
	append(&files, open("b"))
}
```

### destroy append spread

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

main :: proc() {
	a, b: [dynamic]File
	append(&a, ..b[:])
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
append would copy each File
```

`append(&a, ..b[:])` copies each element of `b` into `a`, and `b` keeps its own. Move them one at a time:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
main :: proc() {
	a, b: [dynamic]File
	append(&b, open("x"))
	for i in 0..<len(b) do append(&a, move!(b[i]))
	clear(&b)
}
```

### destroy assign at

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

main :: proc() {
	files: [dynamic]File
	assign_at(&files, 0, open("a"))
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
assign_at would overwrite
```

`assign_at` writes over an element without destroying what was there. Grow the array with `resize`, then assign, which destroys the old value:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
main :: proc() {
	files: [dynamic]File
	resize(&files, 1)
	files[0] = open("a")
}
```

### destroy blank

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

main :: proc() {
	_ = open("a")
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
would throw away a File without destroying it
```

`_ = open("a")` throws the value away, so nothing would destroy it. Keep it in a variable, which destroys it at the end of the scope:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
main :: proc() {
	f := open("a")
	_ = f.name
}
```

### destroy borrow proc value

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }

show :: proc(f: File) { fmt.println(f.name) }

main :: proc() {
	sink: proc(#owned f: File) = show
	sink(File{"a"})
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'show' borrows a File in parameter 'f', but the proc type takes it #owned
```

The procedure type takes its parameter `#owned`, so its callers hand the value over and won't destroy it; `show` only borrows it, so nothing would. Declare the parameter `#owned` in `show` too, or use a type that borrows:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
show :: proc(#owned f: File) { fmt.println(f.name) }

main :: proc() {
	sink: proc(#owned f: File) = show
	sink(File{"a"})
}
```

### destroy capture escape

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

logger :: proc() -> closure() {
	f := open("log")
	return proc[f]() { fmt.println(f.name) }
}

main :: proc() { logger()() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure borrows 'f', a File that has impl Destroy, and is returned
```

A closure that captures a destructible value by value borrows it, so it can't outlive the procedure that owns the value. Share the value through an `Rc`, which the closure can own a copy of on the heap, or keep the closure local:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
```

### destroy capture escape call

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

callbacks: [dynamic]closure()

remember :: proc(cb: closure()) { append(&callbacks, cb) }

setup :: proc() {
	f := open("log")
	remember(proc[f]() { fmt.println(f.name) })
}

main :: proc() { setup() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
this closure borrows 'f', a File that has impl Destroy, and is passed to remember
```

`remember` keeps its closure in a global, so the closure can't borrow `f`, which `setup` destroys when it returns. Capture what the callback needs, rather than the value with a destructor:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
callbacks: [dynamic]closure()

remember :: proc(cb: closure()) { append(&callbacks, cb) }

setup :: proc() {
	f := open("log")
	name := f.name
	remember(proc[name]() { fmt.println(name) })
}

main :: proc() { setup() }
```

A map's keys are copied around as it grows, so they can't be destructible. Key the map by something the value holds, such as its name:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
main :: proc() {
	m: map[string]int
	f := open("a")
	m[f.name] = 1
	fmt.println(len(m))
}
```

### destroy move loop value

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

main :: proc() {
	files: [dynamic]File
	append(&files, open("a"))
	kept: [dynamic]File
	for f in files do append(&kept, move!(f))
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
is a loop value, which borrows each element
```

`for f in files` borrows each element, so it can't move one. Loop over the indexes, and move each element out of the array, which leaves it zero:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
main :: proc() {
	files: [dynamic]File
	append(&files, open("a"))
	kept: [dynamic]File
	for i in 0..<len(files) do append(&kept, move!(files[i]))
}
```

### destroy move param

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) {}
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }

keep :: proc(f: File) -> File {
	return move!(f)
}

main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'f' is a parameter, which is borrowed, so it can't be moved; declare it #owned
```

A by-value parameter is borrowed, so its owner is the caller and it can't be moved. Declare it `#owned` to take it over:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
keep :: proc(#owned f: File) -> File {
	return move!(f)
}

main :: proc() {}
```

### destroy move value

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) {}
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }

open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

main :: proc() {
	f := move!(open("a"))
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
move! takes a variable, field or element, which it leaves zero
```

`move!` leaves what it moves from zero, so it needs a variable, field or element. A new value needs no `move!`:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
main :: proc() {
	f := open("a")
	_ = f.name
}
```

### destroy multi assign

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

main :: proc() {
	f := open("a")
	g := open("b")
	f, g = open("c"), open("d")
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
assigning several values at once
```

Assigning several destructible values in one statement isn't supported yet. Assign them one at a time:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
main :: proc() {
	f := open("a")
	g := open("b")
	f = open("c")
	g = open("d")
}
```

### destroy owned copy

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) {}
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }

consume :: proc(#owned x: File) {}

main :: proc() {
	f := File{"a"}
	consume(f)
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'f' is a File, which has impl Destroy, and passing it to #owned parameter 'x' would copy it; both copies would be destroyed. Move it there with move!(f)
```

An `#owned` parameter takes the value over, so passing a variable would leave two owners. Move it there:

```vidar
File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) {}
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }

consume :: proc(#owned x: File) {}

main :: proc() {
	f := File{"a"}
	consume(move!(f))
}
```

### destroy owned proc value

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }

consume :: proc(#owned f: File) { fmt.println("consumed", f.name) }
apply :: proc(use: proc(File), f: File) { use(f) }

main :: proc() {
	f := File{"a"}
	apply(consume, f)
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'consume' takes a File #owned in parameter 'f', but the proc type it is used as borrows it
```

`consume` destroys its parameter, but callers of a `proc(File)` keep and destroy what they pass, so the file would be destroyed twice. Make the procedure type say `#owned` too, or make `consume` borrow:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
consume :: proc(#owned f: File) { fmt.println("consumed", f.name) }
apply :: proc(use: proc(#owned f: File), #owned f: File) { use(move!(f)) }

main :: proc() {
	f := File{"a"}
	apply(consume, move!(f))
}
```

### destroy owned variadic

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }

close_all :: proc(#owned fs: ..File) {
	fmt.println(len(fs))
}

main :: proc() {
	close_all(File{"a"})
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'fs' can't be #owned: a variadic parameter is a slice
```

A variadic parameter is a slice of values the caller keeps, so it can't be taken over. Take a dynamic array `#owned` instead:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
close_all :: proc(#owned fs: [dynamic]File) {
	fmt.println(len(fs))
}

main :: proc() {
	fs: [dynamic]File
	append(&fs, File{"a"})
	close_all(move!(fs))
}
```

### destroy pop safe

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

main :: proc() {
	files: [dynamic]File
	pop_safe(&files)
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
that pop_safe() returns is thrown away
```

`pop_safe` returns the element it removed, and dropping that result would leak it. Keep it:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
#
main :: proc() {
	files: [dynamic]File
	append(&files, open("a"))
	if f, ok := pop_safe(&files); ok do fmt.println(f.name)
}
```

### destroy range literal

This program doesn't compile:

```text,error-output
would copy one File into each element
```

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }
```

### destroy slice literal

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
```

```text,error-output
in this slice literal
```

A slice literal would be the only owner of its elements, and a slice never destroys them. Build a dynamic array:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }

# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

	append(&files, open("a"), open("b"))
```

### destroy temporary

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:fmt"

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { fmt.println("close", f.name) }
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

show :: proc(f: File) { fmt.println(f.name) }

main :: proc() {
	show(open("a"))
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
is a temporary, so it would never be destroyed
```

`show` borrows its parameter, so the file passed straight into it has no owner, and would never be destroyed. Keep it in a variable first:

```vidar
# File :: struct { name: string }
# file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) { if f.name != "" do fmt.println("close", f.name) }
# impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
# open :: proc(name: string) -> File { return File{name} }

show :: proc(f: File) { fmt.println(f.name) }

main :: proc() {
	f := open("a")
	show(f)
}
```

### destroy unimported

This program doesn't compile:

<span class="filename">Filename: files/files.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package files

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) {}
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
```

<span class="filename">Filename: main.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
import "core:fmt"
import "mid"
```

```vidar,ignore
import "../files"

get :: proc() -> files.File { return files.File{"mid"} }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
destroyed by 'file_destroy' in package 'files'; import that package in this file
```

`main` holds a `files.File`, so it destroys one, and the generated code calls `file_destroy` from package `files`. Odin needs an import for that. Import the package in the file that holds the value, even if nothing else in the file names it:

```vidar,project=err-destroy-unimported,file=main.vidar
package main

import "core:fmt"
import "files"
import "mid"

main :: proc() {
	f := mid.get()
	fmt.println(f.name)
}
```

```vidar,project=err-destroy-unimported,file=mid/mid.vidar
package mid

import "../files"

get :: proc() -> files.File { return files.File{"mid"} }
```

```vidar,project=err-destroy-unimported,file=files/files.vidar
package files

File :: struct { name: string }
file_destroy :: proc(f: ^File) {}
impl Destroy for File { destroy = file_destroy }
```

## Error handling

### catch must leave scope

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }
main :: proc() {
	x := f() catch err {
		_ = err
	}
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
a 'catch' block after a declaration or assignment must leave the scope
```

After a declaration or assignment, the variables would be used unset if the `catch` block fell through, so it must leave the scope: `return`, `break`, `continue` or a panic.

```vidar
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }

main :: proc() {
	x := f() catch err {
		fmt.println(err)
		return
	}
	_ = x
}
```

### catch on compound assign

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }
main :: proc() {
	x := 0
	x += f() catch unreachable
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'catch' goes after a call
```

`catch` follows a call that is the whole right-hand side of `:=` or `=`, or a call statement. Catch the call first, then use its value:

```vidar
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }

main :: proc() {
	x := 0
	y := f() catch unreachable
	x += y
	_ = x
}
```

### catch typed decl

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }
main :: proc() {
	x: int = f() catch unreachable
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'catch' needs a plain 'x := f()' declaration
```

`catch` declares its names the way `:=` does, from the call's results; a declared type isn't allowed. Declare with `:=`, and convert afterwards if needed:

```vidar
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }

main :: proc() {
	x := f() catch unreachable
	_ = x
}
```

### errdefer no results

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
import "core:fmt"
main :: proc() {
	errdefer fmt.println("x")
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'errdefer' needs a procedure that returns an error (or a bool) as its last result
```

`errdefer` runs when the procedure returns a failure, which it can only tell from a last result that is an error or a `bool`. Use `defer`, or give the procedure an error result:

```vidar
Error :: enum { None, Failed }

run :: proc() -> Error {
	errdefer fmt.println("failed")
	return .None
}

main :: proc() { run() }
```

### or return ambiguous

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
f :: proc() -> (int, bool) { return 5, true }
g :: proc() -> (r: int, ok: bool) {
	x := f() or_return - 1
	return x, true
}
main :: proc() { _, _ = g() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
ambiguous '-' after 'or_return'
```

`f() or_return - 1` could mean "return `-1` as the error" or "subtract 1 from the result". Parenthesize the one you mean:

```vidar
f :: proc() -> (int, bool) { return 5, true }

g :: proc() -> (r: int, ok: bool) {
	x := (f() or_return) - 1
	return x, true
}

main :: proc() { _, _ = g() }
```

### or return value nested

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }
g :: proc(x: int) -> int { return x }
h :: proc() -> Error {
	_ = g(f() or_return .Bad)
	return .None
}
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'or_return <value>' must be the whole right-hand side
```

`or_return value` follows a call that is the whole right-hand side. Get the value in a statement of its own:

```vidar
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }
g :: proc(x: int) -> int { return x }

h :: proc() -> Error {
	v := f() or_return .Bad
	_ = g(v)
	return .None
}

main :: proc() {}
```

### or return value no results

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }
main :: proc() {
	x := f() or_return .Bad
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'or_return' needs a procedure that returns an error (or a bool)
```

`or_return` returns from the procedure with an error, and `main` has no result to return it in. Handle the failure with `catch` instead:

```vidar
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }

main :: proc() {
	x := f() catch err {
		fmt.println(err)
		return
	}
	_ = x
}
```

### or return value typed decl

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }
h :: proc() -> Error {
	x: int = f() or_return .Bad
	return .None
}
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'or_return <value>' needs a plain 'x := f()' declaration
```

`or_return value` declares its names the way `:=` does. Drop the type:

```vidar
Error :: enum { None, Bad }
f :: proc() -> (int, Error) { return 1, .None }

h :: proc() -> Error {
	x := f() or_return .Bad
	_ = x
	return .None
}

main :: proc() {}
```

## Interfaces

### bodiless not method

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
foo :: proc(x: int) ---
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'foo' has no body; only interface methods are declared with '---'
```

Outside a `foreign` block, a procedure without a body (`---`) declares an interface method, and must be listed by an interface. Give the procedure a body, or list it in an interface:

```vidar
foo :: proc(x: int) {}

main :: proc() {}
```

### iface anonymous

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {
	x: interface { area }
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
interfaces must be declared as named constants
```

An interface's methods are declared against its name, so it must be a named constant at file scope:

```vidar
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---

main :: proc() {
	x: Shape
	_ = x
}
```

### iface arrow call

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return 1 }
impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
main :: proc() {
	q := Sq{}
	s: Shape = &q
	_ = s->area()
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
call interface methods as procs: area(s)
```

Interface methods are procedures, called with the value first:

```vidar
# Shape :: interface { area }
# area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
# Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
# sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return q.s * q.s }
# impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
#
main :: proc() {
	q := Sq{2}
	s: Shape = &q
	_ = area(s)
}
```

### iface bad arity

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Shape :: interface { scale }
scale :: proc(s: Shape, k: f64) ---
Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
sq_scale :: proc(q: ^Sq) { q.s *= 2 }
impl Shape for Sq { scale = sq_scale }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'sq_scale' must take ^Sq plus 1 parameter(s) to implement 'scale'
```

An implementation takes the receiver plus every other parameter of the method, here `k`:

```vidar
Shape :: interface { scale }
scale :: proc(s: Shape, k: f64) ---
Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
sq_scale :: proc(q: ^Sq, k: f64) { q.s *= k }
impl Shape for Sq { scale = sq_scale }

main :: proc() {}
```

### iface bad receiver

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
sq_area :: proc(q: Sq) -> f64 { return q.s * q.s }
impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
the first parameter of 'sq_area' must have type ^Sq to implement 'area'
```

An implementation takes a pointer to the type first, so that methods can change the value:

```vidar
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return q.s * q.s }
impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }

main :: proc() {}
```

### iface duplicate impl

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return 1 }
impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'Sq' already implements 'Shape'
```

A type implements an interface once. Remove the second `impl`:

```vidar
# Shape :: interface { area }
# area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
# Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
# sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return q.s * q.s }
# impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
#
main :: proc() {}
```

### iface empty

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Shape :: interface {}
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
interface 'Shape' has no methods
```

An interface with no methods would have nothing to call. List its methods:

```vidar
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---

main :: proc() {}
```

### iface extends conflicting impls

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
A :: interface { a }
a :: proc(x: A) ---
B :: interface { using A, b }
b :: proc(x: B) ---
T :: struct {}
t_a :: proc(t: ^T) {}
t_a2 :: proc(t: ^T) {}
t_b :: proc(t: ^T) {}
impl B for T { a = t_a, b = t_b }
impl A for T { a = t_a2 }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'T' implements 'A' twice, binding 'a' differently
```

`impl B for T` already implements `A` for `T`, since `B` extends it, and binds `a` to `t_a`. A second `impl A for T` binding it differently would make `a(&t)` mean two things. Drop the second impl, or bind the same procedure:

```vidar
A :: interface { a }
a :: proc(x: A) ---
B :: interface { using A, b }
b :: proc(x: B) ---
T :: struct {}
t_a :: proc(t: ^T) {}
t_b :: proc(t: ^T) {}
impl B for T { a = t_a, b = t_b }

main :: proc() {}
```

### iface extends cycle

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
A :: interface { using B, a }
a :: proc(x: A) ---
B :: interface { using A, b }
b :: proc(x: B) ---
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
interface 'A' extends itself: A -> B -> A
```

An interface can't include itself, even through another one. Move the shared methods into a third interface that both extend:

```vidar
Base :: interface { base }
base :: proc(x: Base) ---
A :: interface { using Base, a }
a :: proc(x: A) ---
B :: interface { using Base, b }
b :: proc(x: B) ---

main :: proc() {}
```

### impl generic concrete receiver

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output

```

A generic impl covers every `Box(T)`, so it needs procedures that take any `^Box($T)`. For one instance, write an impl for that instance instead:

```vidar
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
Box :: struct($T: typeid) { v: T }
int_area :: proc(b: ^Box(int)) -> f64 { return f64(b.v) }
impl Shape for Box(int) { area = int_area }

main :: proc() {}
```

### impl generic overlap

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
Box :: struct($T: typeid) { v: T }
box_area :: proc(b: ^Box($T)) -> f64 { return f64(b.v) }
int_area :: proc(b: ^Box(int)) -> f64 { return 1 }
impl Shape for Box($T) { area = box_area }
impl Shape for Box(int) { area = int_area }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
impls of 'Shape' for 'Box($T)' and 'Box(int)' overlap
```

`Box($T)` already covers `Box(int)`, so a call on a `Box(int)` would have two implementations. Keep one: the generic impl can handle `int` itself, with a `when` on `T`:

```vidar
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
Box :: struct($T: typeid) { v: T }
box_area :: proc(b: ^Box($T)) -> f64 {
	when T == int do return 1
	else do return f64(b.v)
}
impl Shape for Box($T) { area = box_area }

main :: proc() {}
```
