The message contains:

```text,error-output
a loop over a Pool takes one value: for x in pool (there is no index)
```

A `Pool` is an array per type, so there's no one index across it. Count in the loop if you need one:

```vidar
# Shape :: interface { area }
# area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
# Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
# sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return q.s * q.s }
# impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
#
main :: proc() {
	p: Pool(Shape)
	defer delete(p)
	i := 0
	for s in p {
		_ = s
		i += 1
	}
}
```

### pool generic impl

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
Box :: struct($T: typeid) { v: T }
box_area :: proc(b: ^Box($T)) -> f64 { return f64(b.v) }
impl Shape for Box($T) { area = box_area }
main :: proc() {
	p: Pool(Shape)
	_ = p
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
Pool(Shape) stores one array per implementing type, and can't for the impl for parametric type 'Box($T)'
```

A `Pool` needs one array type per implementation, and a generic impl covers many. Use a `[dynamic]Shape`:

```vidar
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
Box :: struct($T: typeid) { v: T }
box_area :: proc(b: ^Box($T)) -> f64 { return f64(b.v) }
impl Shape for Box($T) { area = box_area }

main :: proc() {
	shapes: [dynamic]Shape
	defer delete(shapes)
}
```

### pool not interface

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return 1 }
impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
main :: proc() {
	p: Pool(Sq)
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
Pool takes an interface: 'Sq' is not one
```

`Pool` takes an interface, and holds the types that implement it. For values of one type, use a dynamic array:

```vidar
# Shape :: interface { area }
# area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
# Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
# sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return q.s * q.s }
# impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
#
main :: proc() {
	p: Pool(Shape)
	defer delete(p)
	squares: [dynamic]Sq
	defer delete(squares)
}
```

### impl outside cycle

This program doesn't compile:

<span class="filename">Filename: main.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package main
import "shapes"
Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return q.s }
impl shapes.Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
main :: proc() {}
```

<span class="filename">Filename: shapes/shapes.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package shapes
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
impl of 'shapes.Shape' must be in package 'shapes' (or a package in an import cycle with it)
```

An interface's method is one Odin proc group, which must list every implementation, so an `impl` lives in the interface's package, or in a package in an import cycle with it. Move the type and its `impl` into `shapes`, or have `shapes` import this package back:

```vidar,project=err-impl-outside-cycle,file=main.vidar
package main

import "shapes"

main :: proc() {
	q := shapes.Sq{2}
	_ = shapes.area(&q)
}
```

```vidar,project=err-impl-outside-cycle,file=shapes/shapes.vidar
package shapes

Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---

Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return q.s }
impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
```

### pool open iface

This program doesn't compile:

<span class="filename">Filename: main.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package main
import "shapes"
Solid :: interface { using shapes.Shape, volume }
volume :: proc(s: Solid) -> f64 ---
main :: proc() {}
```

<span class="filename">Filename: shapes/shapes.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package shapes
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---
Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return 1 }
impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }
all: Pool(Shape)
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
Pool(Shape) needs every implementation of 'Shape' to be known, but 'Solid' in package 'main' extends it
```

A `Pool(Shape)` keeps one array per type that implements `Shape`, so it needs all of them, and an interface in another package that extends `Shape` could add more. Use a `[dynamic]Shape` for the open interface, or keep the extension in `shapes`:

```vidar,project=err-pool-open-iface,file=main.vidar
package main

import "shapes"

Solid :: interface { using shapes.Shape, volume }
volume :: proc(s: Solid) -> f64 ---

main :: proc() {}
```

```vidar,project=err-pool-open-iface,file=shapes/shapes.vidar
package shapes

Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---

Sq :: struct { s: f64 }
sq_area :: proc(q: ^Sq) -> f64 { return 1 }
impl Shape for Sq { area = sq_area }

all: [dynamic]Shape
```

## Optimization attributes

### memo and no memo

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
@(memo, no_memo)
f :: proc(n: int) -> int { return n }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(memo) and @(no_memo) contradict each other
```

`@(memo)` asks for memoization and `@(no_memo)` forbids it. Keep the one you mean:

```vidar
@(memo)
f :: proc(n: int) -> int { return n }

main :: proc() {}
```

### memo bad key

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
@(memo)
total :: proc(xs: []int) -> int { return 0 if len(xs) == 0 else xs[0] + total(xs[1:]) }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(memo) can't apply: '[]int' can't be a map key here
```

The memo table is keyed by the parameters, and a slice can't be a map key. Pass something that can, such as an index into the slice:

```vidar
@(memo)
total_from :: proc(i: int) -> int { return 0 if i >= 5 else i + total_from(i + 1) }

main :: proc() { _ = total_from(0) }
```

### no alloc chain

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

World :: struct { ids: [dynamic]int }

push :: proc(w: ^World, id: int) { append(&w.ids, id) }
spawn :: proc(w: ^World) { push(w, len(w.ids)) }

@(no_alloc)
step :: proc(w: ^World) { if len(w.ids) < 10 do spawn(w) }

main :: proc() {
	w: World
	step(&w)
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(no_alloc) 'step' can allocate: append, reached through step -> spawn -> push at no_alloc_chain.vidar:6
```

`step` doesn't allocate itself, but it calls `spawn`, which calls `push`, which appends. Move the allocation out of the `@(no_alloc)` path: here, reserve room up front and only fill it in `step`:

```vidar
World :: struct { ids: [16]int, count: int }

push :: proc(w: ^World, id: int) { w.ids[w.count] = id; w.count += 1 }
spawn :: proc(w: ^World) { push(w, w.count) }

@(no_alloc)
step :: proc(w: ^World) { if w.count < 10 do spawn(w) }

main :: proc() {
	w: World
	step(&w)
}
```

### no alloc closure

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

@(no_alloc)
apply :: proc(x: int, f: closure(int) -> int) -> int { return f(x) }

main :: proc() { _ = apply(1, proc[](x: int) -> int { return x }) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(no_alloc) 'apply' can't be checked: calls 'f' through a closure, whose targets aren't known
```

Vidar can't know what a closure parameter will call, so it can't promise `apply` doesn't allocate. Take a plain procedure it can follow, or drop the attribute:

```vidar
double :: proc(x: int) -> int { return x * 2 }

@(no_alloc)
apply :: proc(x: int) -> int { return double(x) }

main :: proc() { _ = apply(1) }
```

### no alloc core

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:strings"

@(no_alloc)
name :: proc(s: string) -> string { return strings.clone(s) }

main :: proc() { _ = name("x") }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(no_alloc) 'name' can allocate: strings.clone
```

`strings.clone` allocates a copy. Return the string itself, or have the caller pass a buffer:

```vidar
@(no_alloc)
name :: proc(s: string) -> string { return s }

main :: proc() { _ = name("x") }
```

### no alloc interface

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---

Small :: struct { r: f64 }
Big :: struct { r: f64 }

small_area :: proc(s: ^Small) -> f64 { return s.r }
big_area :: proc(b: ^Big) -> f64 {
	copy := new_clone(b^)
	defer free(copy)
	return copy.r
}

impl Shape for Small { area = small_area }
impl Shape for Big { area = big_area }

@(no_alloc)
total :: proc(xs: []Shape) -> (t: f64) {
	for x in xs do t += area(x)
	return
}

main :: proc() { _ = total(nil) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(no_alloc) 'total' can allocate: new_clone, reached through total -> big_area at no_alloc_interface.vidar:12
```

One implementation of `area`, `big_area`, allocates, and `total` might call it. Remove the allocation from the implementation:

```vidar
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---

Small :: struct { r: f64 }
Big :: struct { r: f64 }

small_area :: proc(s: ^Small) -> f64 { return s.r }
big_area :: proc(b: ^Big) -> f64 { return b.r }

impl Shape for Small { area = small_area }
impl Shape for Big { area = big_area }

@(no_alloc)
total :: proc(xs: []Shape) -> (t: f64) {
	for x in xs do t += area(x)
	return
}

main :: proc() { _ = total(nil) }
```

### no alloc make

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

@(no_alloc)
squares :: proc(n: int) -> []int {
	out := make([]int, n)
	for i in 0..<n do out[i] = i * i
	return out
}

main :: proc() { _ = squares(3) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(no_alloc) 'squares' can allocate: make
```

`make` allocates. Take the output buffer from the caller instead:

```vidar
@(no_alloc)
squares :: proc(out: []int) {
	for i in 0..<len(out) do out[i] = i * i
}

main :: proc() {
	buf: [3]int
	squares(buf[:])
}
```

### no alloc map

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

@(no_alloc)
count :: proc(m: ^map[string]int, word: string) { m[word] = m[word] + 1 }

main :: proc() {
	m: map[string]int
	count(&m, "a")
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(no_alloc) 'count' can allocate: an insert into a map
```

Inserting into a map can grow it. Count into something of fixed size, or drop the attribute:

```vidar
@(no_alloc)
count :: proc(counts: ^[26]int, word: string) {
	if len(word) > 0 && word[0] >= 'a' && word[0] <= 'z' do counts[word[0] - 'a'] += 1
}

main :: proc() {
	counts: [26]int
	count(&counts, "a")
}
```

### no alloc not proc

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

@(no_alloc)
limit := 3

main :: proc() { _ = limit }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(no_alloc) goes on a proc declaration with a body
```

`@(no_alloc)` describes a procedure. Put it on one:

```vidar
limit := 3

@(no_alloc)
get_limit :: proc() -> int { return limit }

main :: proc() { _ = get_limit() }
```

### no alloc unlisted

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "core:os"

@(no_alloc)
load :: proc() -> bool {
	_, ok := os.read_entire_file("x")
	return ok
}

main :: proc() { _ = load() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'os.read_entire_file' (core:os) isn't on the list of procs known not to allocate
```

Vidar only trusts `core:` procedures it knows don't allocate, and `os.read_entire_file` does. Read outside the `@(no_alloc)` procedure, and pass the data in:

```vidar
@(no_alloc)
count_lines :: proc(data: []byte) -> (n: int) {
	for b in data do if b == '\n' do n += 1
	return
}

main :: proc() { _ = count_lines(transmute([]byte)string("a\nb\n")) }
```

### no table not proc

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
@(no_table)
X :: 3
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(no_table) goes on a proc declaration with a body: name :: proc(...) { ... }
```

`@(no_table)` describes a procedure. Put it on one:

```vidar
X :: 3

@(no_table)
f :: proc(b: u8) -> int { return int(b) + X }

main :: proc() {}
```

### specialize and no specialize

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
@(specialize, no_specialize)
f :: proc(n: int) -> int { return n }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(specialize) and @(no_specialize) contradict each other
```

`@(specialize)` asks for specialized copies and `@(no_specialize)` forbids them. Keep the one you mean:

```vidar
@(specialize)
f :: proc(n: int) -> int { return n }

main :: proc() {}
```

### specialize and table

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
@(specialize, table)
f :: proc(b: bool) -> int { return 1 }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
a proc is at most one of @(specialize), @(table) and @(memo)
```

Each of these attributes replaces the procedure's body in its own way, so only one can apply. Pick one:

```vidar
@(table)
f :: proc(b: bool) -> int { return 1 }

main :: proc() {}
```

### specialize not proc

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
@(specialize)
N :: 5
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(specialize) goes on a proc declaration with a body: name :: proc(...) { ... }
```

`@(specialize)` describes a procedure. Put it on one:

```vidar
N :: 5

@(specialize)
scale :: proc(x, k: int) -> int { return x * k }

main :: proc() { _ = scale(N, 2) }
```

### table three params

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
@(table)
add :: proc(a, b, c: u8) -> int { return int(a) + int(b) + int(c) }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(table) needs a proc with one or two parameters and one result
```

A table has one entry per combination of inputs, so it takes one or two small parameters. Split the procedure, or drop the attribute:

```vidar
@(table)
add :: proc(a, b: u8) -> int { return int(a) + int(b) }

main :: proc() {}
```

### table two params enum

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
Color :: enum { Red, Green }
@(table)
shade :: proc(c: Color, dark: bool) -> int { return int(c) * (2 if dark else 1) }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(table) with two parameters needs both of type bool, u8 or i8
```

A two-dimensional table takes two parameters of type `bool`, `u8` or `i8`. Convert the enum, or make it the only parameter:

```vidar
Color :: enum { Red, Green }

@(table)
shade :: proc(c: u8, dark: bool) -> int { return int(c) * (2 if dark else 1) }

main :: proc() { _ = shade(u8(Color.Green), true) }
```

### table wide param

This program doesn't compile:

```vidar,ignore
package main
@(table)
sq :: proc(a: int) -> int { return a * a }
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
@(table) needs a parameter of type bool, u8, i8 or an enum, not int
```

A table stores one result per possible input, which is fine for a `u8` (256) and not for an `int`. Narrow the parameter, or drop the attribute:

```vidar
@(table)
sq :: proc(a: u8) -> int { return int(a) * int(a) }

main :: proc() {}
```

## Packages and imports

### collection missing dir

This program doesn't compile:

<span class="filename">Filename: main.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "lib:thing"

main :: proc() {}
```

<span class="filename">Filename: vidar.toml</span>

```toml
[collections]
lib = "./nowhere"
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
cannot find a package at 'lib:thing'
```

`vidar.toml` maps `lib` to a directory that doesn't exist, or that has no package called `thing` in it. Point the collection at the directory that holds the package:

```toml,project=err-collection-missing-dir,file=vidar.toml
[collections]
lib = "./vendor"
```

```vidar,project=err-collection-missing-dir,file=main.vidar
package main

import "lib:thing"

main :: proc() { _ = thing.answer }
```

```vidar,project=err-collection-missing-dir,file=vendor/thing/thing.vidar
package thing

answer :: 42
```

### missing member

This program doesn't compile:

<span class="filename">Filename: lib/lib.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package lib
x :: 1
```

<span class="filename">Filename: main.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package main
import "lib"
main :: proc() { _ = lib.nope }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
package 'lib' has no member 'nope'
```

The package has no declaration of that name: check the spelling, or that it's declared in the package you imported.

```vidar,project=err-missing-member,file=main.vidar
package main

import "lib"

main :: proc() { _ = lib.x }
```

```vidar,project=err-missing-member,file=lib/lib.vidar
package lib

x :: 1
```

### missing package

This program doesn't compile:

<span class="filename">Filename: main.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package main
import "nowhere"
main :: proc() {}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
cannot find a package at 'nowhere'
```

A relative import names a directory, relative to the importing file, and there's no package there. Check the path:

```vidar,project=err-missing-package,file=main.vidar
package main

import "util"

main :: proc() { _ = util.ok }
```

```vidar,project=err-missing-package,file=util/util.vidar
package util

ok :: true
```

### package goroutines disabled

This program doesn't compile:

<span class="filename">Filename: main.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package main

import "vidar:sched"

main :: proc() {
	sched.go(proc[]() {})
}
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
goroutines are disabled for now: 'vidar:sched' can't be imported
```

Goroutines are disabled for now, because they crash too often on some platforms. To use `vidar:sched` anyway, set `VIDAR_GOROUTINES=1` in the environment:

```bash
VIDAR_GOROUTINES=1 vidar run .
```

### package name mismatch

This program doesn't compile:

<span class="filename">Filename: main.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package main
main :: proc() {}
```

<span class="filename">Filename: z_other.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package other
x :: 1
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
package 'other' does not match package 'main'
```

Every file in a directory belongs to the same package and starts with the same `package` line. Change the line, or move the file to a directory of its own:

```vidar,project=err-package-name-mismatch,file=main.vidar
package main

main :: proc() { _ = x }
```

```vidar,project=err-package-name-mismatch,file=z_other.vidar
package main

x :: 1
```

### private macro

This program doesn't compile:

<span class="filename">Filename: lib/lib.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package lib
@(private) twice :: proc!(n: int) -> int { return n * 2 }
```

<span class="filename">Filename: main.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package main
import "lib"
main :: proc() { _ = lib.twice!(2) }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'lib.twice' is private to package 'lib'
```

`@(private)` keeps a declaration, macros included, inside its package. Remove the attribute to share it:

```vidar,project=err-private-macro,file=main.vidar
package main

import "lib"

main :: proc() { _ = lib.twice!(2) }
```

```vidar,project=err-private-macro,file=lib/lib.vidar
package lib

twice :: proc!(n: int) -> int { return n * 2 }
```

### private member

This program doesn't compile:

<span class="filename">Filename: lib/lib.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package lib
@(private) secret :: proc() -> int { return 1 }
```

<span class="filename">Filename: main.vidar</span>

```vidar,ignore
package main
import "lib"
main :: proc() { _ = lib.secret() }
```

The message contains:

```text,error-output
'lib.secret' is private to package 'lib'
```

`@(private)` keeps a declaration inside its package. Remove the attribute, or call a public procedure that uses it:

```vidar,project=err-private-member,file=main.vidar
package main

import "lib"

main :: proc() { _ = lib.reveal() }
```

```vidar,project=err-private-member,file=lib/lib.vidar
package lib

@(private) secret :: proc() -> int { return 1 }

reveal :: proc() -> int { return secret() }
```
